item.title: Microsoft Edge Hacked With Logic Bugs Only in a $175,000 Pwn2Own Chain
item.description:
A single web page took over a fully patched Windows computer straight through Microsoft Edge, and the break-in paid 175,000 dollars at a hacking contest. The person who got hit only opened the page. The break-in chained 5 flaws with 2 built-in Windows features and no memory bug at all; the features worked as built, and the holes sat in the checks around them.

The page asked for no download and no file to run, and the browser never crashed. It loaded the way a page loads, and by the time it finished, code chosen by the attacker was running on the machine with the same rights as the person in front of it.

This was done in the open at Pwn2Own Berlin, the contest where researchers attack fully updated software in front of a room and get paid for each break-in that lands. The Edge attack paid 175,000 dollars. The payout drew the headlines, but the method is what made it strange, because the attack ran on logic from the first step to the last, with no memory corruption at any point.

That difference is the heart of it. Almost always, breaking out of a browser has meant finding a memory bug. That is a spot where the program gets pushed into writing data where it does not belong, so an attacker can wedge in their own instructions. Browsers are built with layer on layer to stop exactly that. A logic flaw works another way. Nothing overflows and nothing gets corrupted. Each part does the ordinary thing it was written to do, and the attacker only arranges those ordinary things into an order the designers never planned for. The memory defenses have nothing to catch, because on paper the software behaved.

The holes sat in one place. Edge is built on Chromium, the same engine under Google Chrome, and that engine’s own guardrails mostly held. The weak spots were in what Microsoft bolted on top to make Edge friendlier and more useful for companies: a helper that steers work accounts to the right profile, an automatic sign-in, its own reading mode, its own list of sites allowed to pop up a window. The parts that made Edge convenient were the parts that gave way, one after another.

It starts with being signed in. Since Windows 11 version 25H2, setting up a new computer requires a Microsoft account unless you reach for a workaround, and the simple tricks for skipping it keep getting closed. A feature called OneAuth then signs that account in automatically on Microsoft’s own sites. Opening nothing more than www.microsoft.com is enough for Edge to build a profile and sign the person in, even if they never set one up in the browser. Edge is then signed in to a Microsoft identity as soon as someone opens a Microsoft site.

The first flaw lives in a piece of Edge made for companies. When Edge sees someone signing in to a work account on a Microsoft site, a helper steps in to send them to the right profile. To do that, it takes a web address out of the page and starts a fresh navigation to it, from the browser itself. The researcher noticed that this browser-started navigation did not say which tab it came from, and the engine underneath then falls back to whatever tab is active. That gap turns the helper into a way to run the attacker’s script on any site at all, a hole known as universal cross-site scripting. Because the browser itself launches it, the script even steps over CSP, the rule that normally keeps a page from running code it was never served.

This corner is barely explored. The parts that watch over page navigation account for fewer than 20 of the more than 3,000 flaws that engine has fixed in five years, so few people look there. The fallback that leaks the active tab sits so deep in the shared engine that even its own example code uses it the wrong way, which means the problem is not Edge’s alone. The researcher has said he is close to carrying the same chain over to Chrome itself. What looks like one browser’s mistake points at a seam that other browsers share too.

A hole that needs a click is only half a weapon, so the next job was to fire it with no click at all, and that meant clearing four hurdles. The helper was only supposed to run for a trusted Microsoft site, but its check looked at the wrong window, so the attacker’s page could open a Microsoft login page in a popup and steer that popup from the outside. Popups are blocked by default, except Microsoft kept its own hardcoded list of windows that are always allowed, and borrowing one of those opened the door. The helper needed a signed-in profile, which that automatic sign-in now hands over on its own. And it needed the person’s email address, which a misconfigured setting on Microsoft’s assets.msn.com quietly returned to any page that asked. Four pieces, two of them plain mistakes and two of them built-in conveniences, lined up so the trap springs the moment the page loads.

Running the attacker’s script on a trusted page is still inside the sandbox, the padded room a browser keeps each page locked in so it cannot touch the rest of the computer. That wall is the most important one in a modern browser, and getting past it is what turns a bad web page into a problem for the machine behind it. At this year’s contest in Berlin it was the only browser that fell at all, and the researcher has called browsers the hardest category, because the shared engine’s defenses have been hardened almost to the limit.

The way out ran through Edge’s own reading mode, Immersive Reader, which Microsoft forked from the engine long ago and gave a private address scheme written as read://. The engine keeps a blocklist of its trusted internal pages, the ones not allowed to run a javascript: link, and Microsoft forgot to put read:// on it. From inside that trusted page the script could reach a built-in function meant to zip up diagnostic logs, named zipDiagnosticLogFiles. It had a path flaw and a null-byte trick that together let it write a file anywhere the logged-in user can reach. The first plan was to smuggle in a 64-bit program file and have Edge load it, but the write has to be valid text and a 64-bit program header cannot be formed that way, so that route was a dead end.

The route that did work was a small settings file, protocols.json, that Edge reads to decide which sites may launch which outside programs. Overwriting it let the attacker’s page launch a handler of its own choosing, which is why control of that file was the prize. The attacker pointed it at telnet://. Telnet has not shipped turned on with Windows for years, so Windows went looking for telnet.exe down its list of folders. One folder on that list, the per-user WindowsApps folder, could be written to by the ordinary logged-in user. A tiny 32-bit program dropped there was what Windows found and ran. The exploit came to fewer than 100 lines in total. On the contest stage the browser was restarted to reload the settings file, but the write-up is clear that an attack in the wild would not need even that.

Run back over the chain and look at what each link actually was: a sign-in helper, an automatic login, a reading mode, a diagnostics tool, a list of trusted popups. The features behaved normally, and the flaws sat in the checks wrapped around them. Only one link was not an Edge add-on, the tab-fallback buried in the shared engine. Break any single link and the chain falls over, which is what Microsoft’s three fixes did. The separate pieces stay useful on their own, though, and the researcher calls the browser-process cross-site scripting a fresh attack surface he means to dig into further, so the same ideas could turn up again in a new chain.

Code at the user’s level is already a lot. A program running as the logged-in person can read the documents in that account, reach saved files and browser data, install more software, and start looking for ways to climb higher on the system. The break-in did not need administrator rights to be a serious problem, because the files and data people care about live in the user’s own account anyway. From there, a patient attacker can read the passwords and cookies the browser has saved, copy personal files, watch what gets typed, and wait for a second flaw to lift them to full control of the system.

The timeline shows why none of this was a known weakness. The contest only counts attacks against software that is fully patched and current, so going in, nothing on that stage had a fix waiting. The Edge demo ran on the first day, and Microsoft shipped the repair within a day, on May 15, 2026, in Edge version 148.0.3967.70. The full advisory went public in June, and the chain won an Epic Achievement award at the Pwnie Awards in August. The researcher presented it at HITCON and Hexacon, and on October 28 he put the full write-up on his own blog.

Microsoft split the repair into three tracked fixes and credited the researcher by name. The serious one, CVE-2026-45495, is the remote code execution at the end of the chain, rated 8.8 out of 10, and marked as needing the person to open a page. Two more fixes, both rated 5.4, cover other links in the chain. All three were listed as not public and not seen in the wild before the fix.

The chain was put together by hand, over two months, starting from no experience with modern browser exploitation, by a researcher at the security firm DEVCORE working with the Zero Day Initiative, with no AI anywhere in it. The first flaw sat unused in his notes for weeks, read as a minor redirect, until he saw it was something much larger.

His point in publishing it was plain. With memory bugs the hard part is the exploit, but with logic bugs the hard part is seeing them at all, and once they are seen the chaining is the easy bit. In a year when machines are turning up flaws on their own, a chain this long found entirely by a person shows the hard part is still a human one.

A current copy of Edge is safe from this chain. The method is public because the fix has been out since May, and it has never been used against people.

Checking takes a moment:

  • → Open the ⋯ menu in Edge, then Help and feedback, then About Microsoft Edge, or type edge://settings/help
  • → Let it update, and confirm the version reads 148.0.3967.70 or newer

None of this is only about Edge. The same shape shows up wherever convenience features pile up on a browser, because each one is a moving part, and moving parts can be lined up. A machine can be taken over without being broken, talked into a chain of reasonable things in an order that no sensible person would choose.

Cross-site scripting, the path tricks that read files they should not, and turning a web request into a running shell are things you can practice safely in a lab of your own.

My Ethical Hacking Complete Course Zero to Expert takes you there step by step: reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation and traffic analysis, hands-on, from your first day with no Linux or hacking background.

item.title: Ubuntu Servers Still Wait for a Fix to a 9.8 Linux Kernel Bug That an AI Turned Into a Root Exploit
item.description:
Linux servers on Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 are 18 days behind Debian on a 9.8 kernel bug. 53 minutes, no password, and a server runs commands as root. An AI wrote that exploit, for a flaw that has sat in Linux TCP since 2016.

On November 3, Ubuntu’s own security page for CVE-2026-98432 still lists Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 as Vulnerable, with a short note that work is in progress. The Linux kernel developers released the fix on October 15, and Debian shipped it to its users the next day. SUSE began releasing updates on October 29. Red Hat, which rates the bug Critical, the highest level on its scale, followed on November 1 for its Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10. The three Ubuntu versions still waiting are its long-term support releases, the releases built to run on a server for years, with five years of security updates by default.

The score of 9.8 out of 10 comes from the Linux kernel’s own CVE team. It means the bug can be reached over the network, without an account or a password, and without a person on the server clicking or opening anything.

The flaw came to light through Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models. In a research post published on October 27, its Frontier Red Team wrote that it found the bug with an AI model that has not been released to the public. After a first prompt from the team, the AI wrote a working exploit for it.

That exploit sends packets to a Linux server that has a Multipath TCP listener open. It ends with a shell command of the attacker’s choice running as root, with no login and no action needed on the server’s side. In their test it took 48 minutes to pull a kernel pointer out of the target, and about five more minutes to get the command to run. On the kernel side, the fix names Xinyang Ge, with an anthropic.com address, as the person who reported it.

To see why this works, start with the way a TCP connection opens. A computer that wants to talk to a server sends a small packet called a SYN. The server answers with a SYN-ACK, the computer sends an ACK back, and the connection is open. This is the three-way handshake, and it happens before a server sends back a single web page or login screen. An IPv4 packet can also carry a few extra fields in its header, called IP options, up to 40 bytes of them. When a SYN arrives with options attached, Linux keeps a copy of those options and echoes them back to the sender inside its SYN-ACK.

The trouble starts when the same SYN arrives twice, which is normal on the internet, because a client that hears nothing back in time simply sends its SYN again. A second processor core can then begin building a fresh SYN-ACK from those stored options, while the first core finishes setting up the connection and hands the options over to the new connection without copying them. When that new connection is freed, the options are freed with it, and the second core can still be reading from memory that no longer belongs to the connection. By then the kernel may already have handed that memory to something else.

When the result depends on which of two cores gets there first, that is called a race condition, and here it ends in a use-after-free, right in the code that answers incoming connections, on any port where a server listens.

In the first stage of the exploit, the race makes the kernel read a length field that the attacker controls. The kernel then copies extra bytes into its reply and sends them out, and among them is a kernel pointer, an address that shows where the kernel sits in memory. Linux shuffles that layout each time it starts, a protection called KASLR, so a remote attacker cannot predict it, and one leaked pointer is enough to undo it.

In the second stage, the same use-after-free is used to overwrite a callback pointer, an address the kernel will later jump to, so that it points at a payload the attacker staged earlier. That payload strings together functions that already exist inside the kernel, and the last of them runs the attacker’s shell command as root.

A race like this does not succeed on the first try, and that is where the 48 minutes come from. A lost attempt only breaks that one handshake, without crashing the server, so the attacker can keep sending attempts until one succeeds. The race also makes the attack harder to pull off than the score alone suggests. SUSE scores it 8.1 instead of 9.8, because it rates the attack complexity as high, and Red Hat writes that reliable code execution needs precise control over the kernel heap, the memory the kernel hands out while it runs.

The code change behind this bug is more than ten years old. On October 2, 2015, Eric Dumazet changed the way Linux stores incoming connection requests, so that they sit in the main lookup table while the handshake is still going on. That change shipped in Linux 4.4, released on January 10, 2016, and the kernels released since then carry the flaw. A second path into the same bug arrived in June 2021, through a feature that moves waiting connection requests from one listening socket to another. That feature is turned off by default.

Eleven years after the original change, on October 1, 2026, the same man wrote the fix. The engineer who added the second path in 2021 reviewed it. The patch itself is small: where the kernel used to free the stored options straight away, it now waits until no other processor core can still be reading them, using a method called RCU, which stands for read-copy-update. The options stay in memory for that short window, and only then does the kernel release them.

Multipath TCP, or MPTCP, is a version of TCP that lets one connection run over several network paths at the same time, for example over a wired link and a mobile link together. The exploit from the red team needs a server with an MPTCP listener. Ubuntu builds MPTCP into its 24.04 kernel on all supported architectures, and the Linux kernel turns it on by default.

On top of that, since Go 1.24, released in February 2025, programs written in Go open their listening sockets on Linux with MPTCP by default. A server program built with a recent version of Go, such as the Caddy web server, can therefore be listening with MPTCP on a stock Ubuntu 24.04 kernel without its administrator ever choosing it. The Go security team sent out a warning about exactly this on October 29.

Switching MPTCP off closes the route this one exploit takes, and the flaw itself stays in plain IPv4 TCP. A Red Hat security bulletin states that MPTCP is not required for the bug, and that OpenShift nodes, where MPTCP is disabled, are still affected. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, writes that the fix is not specific to MPTCP.

The reason Ubuntu is behind comes down to which kernel each distribution runs. Debian runs on the 6.12 kernel line, which received the fix in version 6.12.113 on October 15, so Debian only had to package it. Ubuntu 22.04 runs on its own build of the 5.15 line, and 5.15.223 with the fix came out on that same October 15. Ubuntu 24.04 runs on 6.8 and Ubuntu 26.04 on 7.0. The fix from the kernel developers did not come out for those two lines, so the Ubuntu kernel team has to carry it over itself.

That work is done: fixed kernels for 22.04 and 24.04 went into a section of the Ubuntu archive called -proposed on October 26, and the kernel for 26.04 followed on October 28. The -proposed pocket is Ubuntu’s testing area. Packages there are not picked up by a normal update, so a server only receives them when its administrator turns that pocket on by hand. In a blog post on November 2, Ubuntu wrote that the kernels are in qualification testing on more than 2,000 certified servers and devices. They move to the regular updates as soon as those tests are complete, and the post gives no date.

The same blog post describes the CVSS score of 9.8 as a severity of High, one step below Critical. The Ubuntu Server page promises timely patches for critical vulnerabilities to customers of Ubuntu Pro, the paid subscription. The older releases, Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04, only receive security fixes through that subscription, and all three are still listed as fix pending.

An Ubuntu server can be checked in a minute. The first command shows which kernel is running, the second lists the kernel packages that are installed:

1
2

uname -r
dpkg -l 'linux-image*' | grep ^ii

Two more commands show whether a server matches the setup of the published exploit. The first prints 1 when MPTCP is switched on, the second lists the listening sockets that use it, with the program behind each one:

1
2

sysctl net.mptcp.enabled
sudo ss -lnMp

For administrators who want the fixed kernel from the testing pocket now instead of waiting, Ubuntu gives these commands, and says this route is meant for teams that test kernels themselves before rolling them out. They turn on the -proposed pocket and install the kernel from it, and the server needs a restart afterwards. The install line assumes a kernel that was installed through a meta-package:

1
2
3
4

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu
sudo apt update
dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade
sudo reboot

For servers that cannot take that step yet, the same bulletin publishes a firewall rule that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets with IP options, so the bug never gets its input. Save it as cve-2026-98432.nft:

1
2
3
4
5
6

table inet cve_2026_98432 {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept;
        ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop
    }
}

Then test the file and load it, and the last command confirms the table is active:

1
2
3

sudo nft --check --file cve-2026-98432.nft
sudo nft --file cve-2026-98432.nft
sudo nft list table inet cve_2026_98432

The rule has limits, and Ubuntu’s own CVE page spells them out:

  • → It covers the host itself, and containers with their own network setup need the rule applied separately
  • → It is gone after a reboot unless it is added to /etc/nftables.conf
  • → It breaks connections that depend on IPv4 options, such as CIPSO security labels
  • → IPv6 traffic does not need it, because IPv6 is not affected by the main bug

The bulletin calls the rule a way to reduce exposure and not a replacement for the kernel update. Ubuntu’s security team goes further and says the update itself is the only proper fix. Once the fixed kernel is running, the rule comes off again with sudo nft delete table inet cve_2026_98432.

So far there is no report of this bug being used in a successful attack, but the scanning has started. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins wrote on November 3 that a scan on October 30 found about 2.1 million servers reachable over MPTCP on port 443, without showing which of them are patched. Since November 2 his team has seen residential proxies and Russia-based VPN servers probing port 443 with MPTCP, which ordinary scanners do not use, and he suspects attackers looking for this bug. Denial-of-service proof-of-concepts are already circulating, and the exploit from the red team has not been released.

The CVE does not appear in the list of known exploited vulnerabilities kept by CISA, the US cybersecurity agency. Debian already has a fixed kernel, and so do the standard kernels of Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, while SUSE has fixes out for several of its versions with others still in progress. On those systems the fix only takes effect after the update and a reboot, when uname -r shows the new version.

On Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04, a plain sudo apt upgrade will not bring in the fix until it moves out of -proposed. A server there that reports nothing left to update can still be running the vulnerable kernel today.

Linux servers on Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 are 18 days behind Debian on a 9.8 kernel bug. 53 minutes, no password, and a server runs commands as root. An AI wrote that exploit, for a flaw that has sat in Linux TCP since 2016.

On November 3, Ubuntu’s own security page for CVE-2026-98432 still lists Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 as Vulnerable, with a short note that work is in progress. The Linux kernel developers released the fix on October 15, and Debian shipped it to its users the next day. SUSE began releasing updates on October 29. Red Hat, which rates the bug Critical, the highest level on its scale, followed on November 1 for its Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10. The three Ubuntu versions still waiting are its long-term support releases, the releases built to run on a server for years, with five years of security updates by default.

The score of 9.8 out of 10 comes from the Linux kernel’s own CVE team. It means the bug can be reached over the network, without an account or a password, and without a person on the server clicking or opening anything.

The flaw came to light through Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models. In a research post published on October 27, its Frontier Red Team wrote that it found the bug with an AI model that has not been released to the public. After a first prompt from the team, the AI wrote a working exploit for it.

That exploit sends packets to a Linux server that has a Multipath TCP listener open. It ends with a shell command of the attacker’s choice running as root, with no login and no action needed on the server’s side. In their test it took 48 minutes to pull a kernel pointer out of the target, and about five more minutes to get the command to run. On the kernel side, the fix names Xinyang Ge, with an anthropic.com address, as the person who reported it.

To see why this works, start with the way a TCP connection opens. A computer that wants to talk to a server sends a small packet called a SYN. The server answers with a SYN-ACK, the computer sends an ACK back, and the connection is open. This is the three-way handshake, and it happens before a server sends back a single web page or login screen. An IPv4 packet can also carry a few extra fields in its header, called IP options, up to 40 bytes of them. When a SYN arrives with options attached, Linux keeps a copy of those options and echoes them back to the sender inside its SYN-ACK.

The trouble starts when the same SYN arrives twice, which is normal on the internet, because a client that hears nothing back in time simply sends its SYN again. A second processor core can then begin building a fresh SYN-ACK from those stored options, while the first core finishes setting up the connection and hands the options over to the new connection without copying them. When that new connection is freed, the options are freed with it, and the second core can still be reading from memory that no longer belongs to the connection. By then the kernel may already have handed that memory to something else.

When the result depends on which of two cores gets there first, that is called a race condition, and here it ends in a use-after-free, right in the code that answers incoming connections, on any port where a server listens.

In the first stage of the exploit, the race makes the kernel read a length field that the attacker controls. The kernel then copies extra bytes into its reply and sends them out, and among them is a kernel pointer, an address that shows where the kernel sits in memory. Linux shuffles that layout each time it starts, a protection called KASLR, so a remote attacker cannot predict it, and one leaked pointer is enough to undo it.

In the second stage, the same use-after-free is used to overwrite a callback pointer, an address the kernel will later jump to, so that it points at a payload the attacker staged earlier. That payload strings together functions that already exist inside the kernel, and the last of them runs the attacker’s shell command as root.

A race like this does not succeed on the first try, and that is where the 48 minutes come from. A lost attempt only breaks that one handshake, without crashing the server, so the attacker can keep sending attempts until one succeeds. The race also makes the attack harder to pull off than the score alone suggests. SUSE scores it 8.1 instead of 9.8, because it rates the attack complexity as high, and Red Hat writes that reliable code execution needs precise control over the kernel heap, the memory the kernel hands out while it runs.

The code change behind this bug is more than ten years old. On October 2, 2015, Eric Dumazet changed the way Linux stores incoming connection requests, so that they sit in the main lookup table while the handshake is still going on. That change shipped in Linux 4.4, released on January 10, 2016, and the kernels released since then carry the flaw. A second path into the same bug arrived in June 2021, through a feature that moves waiting connection requests from one listening socket to another. That feature is turned off by default.

Eleven years after the original change, on October 1, 2026, the same man wrote the fix. The engineer who added the second path in 2021 reviewed it. The patch itself is small: where the kernel used to free the stored options straight away, it now waits until no other processor core can still be reading them, using a method called RCU, which stands for read-copy-update. The options stay in memory for that short window, and only then does the kernel release them.

Multipath TCP, or MPTCP, is a version of TCP that lets one connection run over several network paths at the same time, for example over a wired link and a mobile link together. The exploit from the red team needs a server with an MPTCP listener. Ubuntu builds MPTCP into its 24.04 kernel on all supported architectures, and the Linux kernel turns it on by default.

On top of that, since Go 1.24, released in February 2025, programs written in Go open their listening sockets on Linux with MPTCP by default. A server program built with a recent version of Go, such as the Caddy web server, can therefore be listening with MPTCP on a stock Ubuntu 24.04 kernel without its administrator ever choosing it. The Go security team sent out a warning about exactly this on October 29.

Switching MPTCP off closes the route this one exploit takes, and the flaw itself stays in plain IPv4 TCP. A Red Hat security bulletin states that MPTCP is not required for the bug, and that OpenShift nodes, where MPTCP is disabled, are still affected. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, writes that the fix is not specific to MPTCP.

The reason Ubuntu is behind comes down to which kernel each distribution runs. Ubuntu 22.04 runs on its own build of the 5.15 line, and 5.15.223 with the fix came out on that same October 15. Ubuntu 24.04 runs on 6.8 and Ubuntu 26.04 on 7.0. The fix from the kernel developers did not come out for those two lines, so the Ubuntu kernel team has to carry it over itself.

3

item.title: Danfoss Fridge Controllers Hacked Again as Freezers Hit 50°C in Ten European Countries
item.description:
Freezers in more than 100 stores across ten countries went warm overnight, some set to 50°C. Three weeks after France. The boxes running them were still online, after the maker told stores to take them off.

It started again on the night of Sunday, November 1. Around midnight, the cooling in stores across Belgium began to change. Fridges and freezers switched to defrost, some shut down completely, and in a few the settings were pushed up until the units were producing heat instead of cold. By Monday morning the same thing had happened in Sweden, Ireland, Luxembourg, Estonia, Finland, Italy, Portugal, the Netherlands and Denmark.

At an ICA supermarket in Sjöbo, in the south of Sweden, the morning staff found the fridges and freezers set to 50°C, which is 122°F. The store posted on Facebook that the cooling had been hacked. The manager told reporters they could not change the temperatures back, and the store stayed closed that morning. On the island of Öland, the manager of a small village shop found a puddle of water on the floor and the cooling set to 55°C. The shop had no fresh or frozen food left to sell.

The most stores were hit in Belgium. By Monday afternoon, local media had counted at least 76 supermarkets and other shops with refrigeration problems. Delhaize said an “IT incident” had affected the cooling in several dozen of its stores, around 40 according to most reports. Carrefour counted 15 of its 700 locations in the country. Its spokesman put it plainly: “It’s a cyberattack, there is no other reason.” Five franchised Spar shops, around 15 Intermarché stores and the IKEA in Mons were hit as well.

The losses per store were large. The manager of one store near Brussels called the consequences “catastrophic”. His store threw out all of its fresh and frozen food. Another store had to throw away at least €60,000 worth of food. At a butcher shop south of Antwerp, the fridges climbed to 18°C, and about €15,000 worth of meat was lost.

The list kept growing. In Ireland, 13 supermarkets of one chain had to pull chilled and frozen products from sale. Four stores in Luxembourg were affected. In Estonia, attackers set a freezer in one supermarket to 50°C, but the alarm was answered within ten minutes and the temperature rose only two to three degrees. The chain said it was the last of its stores where the new system was not yet in use.

In Sicily, at least four supermarkets were hit, plus one business in Tuscany. The general director of the group that runs the Sicilian stores said the attack came at 4:00 in the morning. Its chief executive said the attackers got into the remote-control system for the frozen food cases. The Italian government scheduled a cybersecurity meeting with its intelligence services for the next day. In Finland, a few smaller grocery stores recorded strange temperatures, and the chain’s head of security said interference over the network had not been ruled out. In Portugal, seven stores confirmed problems. In the Netherlands, at least 17 businesses were hit, mostly butcher shops and small food stores.

In Denmark, the government’s civil security agency knew of five companies whose cooling systems were hit. They got the attackers out quickly, it said, without major outages. At one food producer, the refrigeration supplier caught the attack, stopped it and then sounded the alarm. In Romania, the national cybersecurity directorate reported a possible attack on six stores of one chain. Around 1:30 in the morning their refrigeration equipment climbed to very high temperatures, and the problem was only noticed at 8:00. The controllers went online through GSM routers, small boxes that connect over the mobile phone network, each with a fixed IP address that could be reached straight from the internet. The software on them was old.

The European Commission reacted the same day. Christophe Hansen, the EU commissioner for agriculture and food, said in a statement: “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.” He called the attack “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it.” Federal prosecutors in Brussels opened a criminal investigation. In Sweden, the National Cybersecurity Centre took up the case, and its head called it serious because the food supply is part of the country’s infrastructure. So far, the attack is unclaimed.

This was the second time in three weeks.

On the night of October 11, it happened in France. The finance minister told parliament that about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets were affected. Some units ran hot for hours before the first employees arrived, the food went in the bin, and the Paris prosecutor’s office spoke of fires. I wrote about that attack on October 13, and about the boxes that made it possible.

A supermarket has many cooling units, from display cases to cold rooms, and above them sits one box that ties them together: the system manager. From its web page, a technician can see the temperature of each unit, change the settings, and plan the defrost cycles. Defrosting is normal. Ice builds up, the unit warms for a while to melt it, and then goes back to cooling. Leave it in defrost, or set the target temperature to 50°C, and the food inside is gone by morning. To let the maintenance company check a store without driving there, that web page was often put straight on the internet.

On Monday, Danfoss confirmed to the Danish broadcaster DR that the incidents in several countries involved its products. After the French attack in October, it had named two controllers: the AK-SM800 and the AK-SC355. The AK-SC355 was phased out in 2016. The AK-SM800 reached its end of life in 2021. Neither gets software or security updates anymore.

A refrigeration company in Estonia said the system attacked there was an older type of Danfoss system. “The signature is the same, but I can’t comment further yet,” its director added. The supermarket chain from Sjöbo said the stores it had affected were all connected to an outside refrigeration control system from Danfoss. Dutch reports said devices from a second maker, an American company, were also among the targets.

So the attackers went back to the same boxes, after two warnings.

  • → October 13. Danfoss wrote to its customers and told them to cut the internet connection of these systems and to restore access only through a secured network. This week, a company spokesperson told the Dutch broadcaster NOS: “Most stores took action at that time, but a small number did not.” In the Netherlands, the spokesperson added, the systems hit on Monday were not on a secured network and still had a default password. On that same October 13, CERT-FR, the French government’s computer emergency team, widened its alert. Besides Danfoss, it now also named the XWEB controllers made by Copeland and Dixell, which do the same job. The second maker that Dutch reports now mention was on the French list three weeks ago.

  • → October 16. The French team updated its alert for the last time. In its current form, one line reads: “Des campagnes d’attaques sont probablement toujours en cours visant ces équipements.” In English: attack campaigns against this equipment are probably still going on. The same alert warns that a factory reset is not enough on an old box that no longer gets patches. The box stays vulnerable and will most likely be broken into again.

  • → October 20 to 30. The security company Lupovis runs decoy controllers on the internet, built to look like Danfoss units and to record who tries to log in. In those ten days it saw login attempts against them, with a peak on October 26. Most of the attempts used the factory default login details, the ones Danfoss documents in public. The decoys rejected them. Somebody was out looking for these boxes a week before the attack. Whether they were the same people who struck on Monday is not known.

  • → November 2, the day itself. The security researcher Kevin Beaumont wrote that he had checked with people involved. In his words: “I’ve confirmed with folks the impacted freezers in the countries impacted today are all mgmt interface facing internet.” Many of them, he added, are end-of-life with no patch available.

One Belgian refrigeration installer, which manages hundreds of these installations, started securing them after the October attack. On Monday its chief executive said around 10 percent were not finished yet, and some of those were in the shops that got hit. He knew of about twenty affected units. According to him, the same weakness was used as in France, and a software update alone does not close it. The boxes also need physical changes, which cost money.

Censys, a company that scans the internet around the clock, counted how many of these boxes are still reachable. It looks for the web page of the Danfoss system manager, the screen called StoreView. Before October 11 it found 1,825 of them in France. On October 14 it was 537. On Monday it was 220. Across the internet, the count is a little over 1,000. Belgium has 138, the Netherlands 51, Sweden 50, Luxembourg 6, Ireland 3 and Estonia 2.

The scan also estimated which software those boxes run. One of the holes I described last time was a hidden second password in the AK-SM 800A, a “code of the day” calculated from the device’s own date and time. Whoever knows the calculation can work out the code and log in without the administrator’s password. That hole, CVE-2025-41450, was fixed in version 4.2 in March 2025. Of the boxes still reachable in France, 45 percent run software older than that. In the Netherlands it is 41 percent, in Sweden 38 percent, in Belgium 28 percent. The version is read from a timestamp the web server gives out, so it is an estimate. And for the two old models that Danfoss named, no fix exists at all, whatever version they run.

How the attackers got in this time has not been made public. A security expert at Zscaler named the two likely ways in to AFP: a known hole in the software, or a login with credentials that had been stolen or leaked. After October, Vincent Strubel, the head of the French national cybersecurity agency ANSSI, put the first attack down to “basic security shortcomings”. The boxes were directly exposed to the internet, and the passwords were weak. An engineer at the French security firm Synacktiv said these systems normally sit on a closed network and “are not supposed to be accessible from the Internet”. Many of them could still be reached by somebody with only basic knowledge, he said. “The attack was not extremely sophisticated.”

Changing a temperature or a defrost schedule is an ordinary function of the system manager. With a working login, an attacker changes it the same way the technician does. In Sweden, the supermarket chain Coop said its affected stores were connected through a 4G mobile network and not through its updated 5G system, and that this made them “more exposed”.

The pattern did not start in Europe.

In the last week of August, freezers at US military commissaries, the supermarkets on military bases, went into defrost overnight. At least six stores confirmed it, from Fort Huachuca in Arizona to Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island. Since my first post, the investigation has grown. The Pentagon says a unit of US Cyber Command is now working on it with other agencies, and the Army’s criminal investigators are working with French law enforcement. That does not prove the same people did both. It is still not public which company made the controllers in those stores, and the military has not confirmed that the systems were broken into.

On the same night as the October attack in France, Ahold Delhaize took systems offline after a separate security problem. The group also reported suspicious activity in its network to Dutch police. Three weeks later, the cooling in dozens of its Belgian stores was tampered with. In October the company said there was no reason to link its incident to the attack in France, and so far nothing connects the two.

By Monday afternoon, some chains reported that their fridges and freezers were working normally again. The installer had pulled the affected units off the network. The stock that had warmed up overnight was already in the bin. Who did it is still unknown, and so is whether they will come back a third time.

item.title: Videostrong Built a Backdoor Into 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes and Sold the Access to Criminals
item.description:
1,472,554 TV boxes and other Android devices in over 170 countries shipped with a backdoor. The owners did nothing wrong. The maker put it in the firmware, at least since 2020, and sold access to criminals.

On November 2, Google’s threat intelligence team named the company behind the backdoor: Videostrong Technology, a manufacturer in China that designs and builds Android TV boxes for its own brands and for other companies. The team writes with high confidence that Videostrong developed the backdoor, put it on its boxes, turned them into a botnet and ran it for profit, as a deliberate campaign by the company itself. The team calls a device maker that infects its own users on purpose an unacceptable breach of trust. Videostrong then sold access to those boxes to other criminal groups, who paid to load their own software onto them.

The count of 1,472,554 comes from TrendAI, which measured the operation between June and October 2026 and found the backdoor in 206 different models of TV boxes, projectors and other Android devices. Its collection had gaps, so the researchers call that number a lower limit. Most of the devices are in Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan. In the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada, the count lies between about 26,000 and 42,000 devices per country. Over those four months, 3,849,226 different home and mobile IP addresses showed up as exit points for internet traffic that other people paid to send through these boxes. A second research team puts the number of devices that contact the operators’ servers on any given day at around half a million.

One of the boxes is the MECOOL KM9PRO Max. Its maker announced it on December 5, 2024, as a 4K streaming box certified by Google and Netflix, and pitched it as a Christmas present. At IFA in Berlin in 2025, Videostrong presented itself as a maker of Google certified and Dolby approved devices. That second research team is Synthient, a company that tracks proxy networks, and its researchers bought a KM9PRO Max in late 2025. They switched on developer mode and connected to it over ADB, the Android Debug Bridge that developers use to control an Android device from a computer, on port 5555. Then they dumped the apps and processes that were running. The backdoor was already there, running with system rights under the name com.oemservice.

Before a box may ship with the Play Store on it, its software has to pass a set of compatibility and security tests. Videostrong scrambled its code so the tests could not see what it did, a trick called obfuscation, and the malicious part only loaded after the buyer switched the box on for the first time. The threat intelligence team writes that Videostrong exploited a gap in those tests, and that the review process has been changed because of it.

The backdoor itself is called x.cpe, and in some builds it runs as com.oemservice. It starts as a small starter program, called a stub, in the system part of the firmware, with the same rights as Android’s own system processes, the level Android calls android.uid.system. When the box boots, the stub looks in a separate partition called /oem/ for the full package and installs it into /data/app/. An owner who finds it there and uninstalls it gets it back at the next restart. As a normal user, there is no way to get rid of it.

When the box starts, it sends its device information to a server under anyevonline[.]com. The server answers with login details for a second server that uses MQTT, a small messaging protocol. From that moment the box keeps a connection open to mqtt.szbboys[.]com on ports 3885, 3886 and 3887, and waits for orders. Each check-in message it sends contains information about the device, and also the e-mail address of the user, if someone is signed in on the box.

Before it installs anything, the backdoor wipes the setting on the box that records what the user agreed to. Then it turns off Play Protect, the scanner that checks apps on Android devices. From there it can install apps without asking, run shell commands and scripts, take screenshots of what is on the TV, send key presses to the box and map the network it sits on with ping and traceroute tests. In the four months of counting, silent install commands reached more than 187,000 devices, and the operators could also collect Wi-Fi and Bluetooth data from the boxes.

The money came from what Videostrong let other companies run on the boxes, and the largest part was proxy software. About 1.33 million of the counted devices were lined up to get that extra software, the proxy and ad fraud modules. A residential proxy sells access to home internet connections. A customer pays, and their traffic goes out onto the internet from a living room, with that household’s IP address on it, while the household has no idea.

The threat intelligence report lists modules from Honeygain and NetNut among the proxy providers, plus six more. Next to the proxies came ad fraud modules that load ads in the background and click on them. Four more backdoors came along as well, among them Moyu and Bird, which researchers had seen before in BadBox, an earlier operation built on backdoored TV boxes. The groups behind those modules also had other ways onto devices, and their servers reach at least 10 million more compromised devices on top of the 1.3 million, according to the same report.

Besides TV boxes, x.cpe also turned up on telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signs.

The oldest x.cpe sample in the researchers’ published list was first seen on December 14, 2020, as version 3.6.5. In late 2024, Videostrong moved the modules that made the money out of x.cpe and into a separate app called com.abc.nexus, possibly in response to earlier enforcement against those older backdoored boxes. Nexus bundled several proxy programs into one app, and the researchers traced it through a series of versions, with proxy providers added and removed along the way.

In August 2026 the operators changed course again, and Nexus was uninstalled from boxes across the botnet. New packages arrived through the messaging connection, named to look like part of Android: com.android.system.ntp and com.android.sso.auth.handler. Several versions of them unpack a file called libexploit.so. That file restarts adbd, the service behind ADB, with root rights and opens a shell through it. The package then uses that shell to copy itself into /system/priv-app/, and writes a permissions file that lets it install packages and reboot the box. Some of the payloads came from a public code repository called Aviciiii/ott, filled with device images and backdoors, which now returns a 404.

The trail to Videostrong runs through Kimwolf, the botnet I wrote about in January, which reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android TV boxes with an open debug port, through a hole in a proxy service. While tracking that botnet, the same researchers saw boxes of this kind getting infected, and MECOOL devices were among them. Boxes like these are popular for pirated streams, and together with the Motion Picture Association, the film industry group that fights piracy, the researchers bought several of them to take apart.

Following the servers, the researchers found that the command server anyevonline[.]com has a subdomain, file.anyevonline[.]com on port 8000, with an open directory that was reachable from the internet without a login. Inside were the backdoors the operators used, and a folder named pdf. In that folder was a signed device declaration from Owen Cao, the R&D director of Videostrong. The domain videostrong.cn points to the same IP address as mqtt.anyevonline[.]com, the operators’ admin panel, where they could see their victims and hand out tasks.

The operators signed the backdoors with Videostrong e-mail addresses. In the list of traces the researchers published, the certificate for the over-the-air updates and the certificate that signs the Yoka apps and the CPE app itself both carry the same address, hong.luo@videostrong.com. The threat intelligence report also lists eleven accounts on a code-hosting site that served the operators’ packages, and one of them is called yf-videostrong.

The message server is called szbboys, and Bboys also shows up in the trademark records of the United States Patent and Trademark Office. There, the MECOOL trademark belongs to Shenzhen Bboys Technology Co., Ltd., on the 5th floor of the Lushi Industry Building in the Bao’an 28 District. The same company holds the US trademarks YOKATV and M8S PLUS.

YOKATV used to belong to Videostrong itself, which registered it in 2016. That registration lapsed, and the office cancelled it on August 4, 2023. On November 25, 2023, the MECOOL trademark holder filed for the same name and got it registered in October 2024. Yokatv.com is one of the storefronts where the researchers found the backdoored devices for sale, and M8S_PLUS is one of the model names on their list. Videostrong’s own website gives its address as the 6th floor of the Lushi Industrial East Building, in that same district.

That website now leads with AI companion robots and products for elderly care. The company sells the HC1 Home Care Hub for elderly care and telehealth, with a 1080p camera and two microphones, and it supports MQTT, the same protocol the backdoor uses. Its KA1 is a smart speaker with an Android TV box inside, and its KA2 is a box with a full HD camera, a microphone array, a speaker and Android TV. MECOOL’s own store sells them as the HomePlus KA1 and the Now KA2, the second one as Google certified video calling on TV.

All three model names appear on the list of 182 model names seen in this campaign. The researchers add that a model name on its own does not prove a device is infected, and nothing on that list shows these are the same products. The HC1 product page says Videostrong does not store or share voice, image or video data from its devices.

Last week, Google took the operation down together with Japan’s National Police Agency and five security companies, among them the two research teams named here. Through legal action, it took down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the boxes and push its modules, along with the command servers of more than a dozen malware families the backdoor loaded onto them. It also cut its ties with Videostrong and banned the company, and any future subsidiary or affiliate, from building certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified makers. Videostrong did not immediately respond to questions from The Register.

The servers are gone, but the backdoor is still on the boxes. It sits in the firmware and puts itself back after a restart, and the owner cannot remove it. The team that counted the boxes says cleaning them needs the vendor or the platform to act, or a new device. The advice from the team that bought the box is shorter: get rid of it, because it may still carry other malware.

The threat intelligence team also points at the shops. Retailers and online marketplaces that sell these boxes share responsibility, it writes, and should demand independent security audits from manufacturers and quickly stop selling devices from the makers caught doing this. The researchers who bought the box go further and want these devices pulled from online stores and marketplaces right away.

To see which box you have, open the settings and look up the model name, then compare it with the list of 182 model names in Synthient’s public research repository on GitHub. With network debugging switched on in the box’s developer options, a computer on the same network can check for the package names from the report:

1
2
3
4
5
6

adb connect 192.168.1.50:5555
adb shell pm list packages oemservice
adb shell pm list packages cpe
adb shell pm list packages abc.nexus
adb shell pm list packages system.ntp
adb shell pm list packages sso.auth

Replace 192.168.1.50 with the IP address of the box. A line that starts with package: means the name is installed. Take a box that shows one of them off the network. Switch network debugging off again when you are done, because an open debugging port on the home network is how the botnet from January got onto boxes like these.

The report gives owners this advice:

  • → Keep the built-in app scanner turned on
  • → Stay away from apps that pay for unused bandwidth or for sharing your internet connection
  • → Buy boxes from brands on the Android TV partner list

On these boxes the first tip does not help, because the backdoor itself sets package_verifier_user_consent to -1, and that switches the scanner off. The box from the start of this story was advertised as Google certified.

Which devices on your own network answer on port 5555, and which one keeps talking to the internet while the TV is switched off?

item.title: mSecure Password Manager Tells Customers to Replace Their Passwords, 2FA and Passkeys Without Saying Why
item.description:
Customers with close to 1,000 logins in one password manager got one email: change the passwords, reset the 2FA, remove the passkeys. No reason given. A German government test flagged it 11 months earlier.

After a few years, almost everything ends up in your password manager. The login for your bank, your email, your work accounts, the six-digit codes for two-factor login, and lately your passkeys as well. You remember one master password, and the app remembers the rest.

On November 3, customers of the password manager mSecure opened an email from mSeven Software, the company in Lake Oswego, Oregon, that makes the app. Former customers, who had stopped using it, got the same email.

It said the company had “recently learned of suspicious activity” connected to mSecure. They had started an investigation, taken steps to limit the damage, and brought in outside security experts. Then came the advice. Because of the potential security implications, you should immediately protect the confidential information you keep in the app. That could mean changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication, or removing existing passkeys.

The last line read: “We regret any inconvenience that this may cause.”

That was all. Nothing about what the suspicious activity was, when it happened, which systems were involved, or whether customer data had been taken. The email gave so little that customers on the forum asked each other whether it was genuine or a phishing attempt.

On mSecure’s own support forum, customers started counting what that advice meant for them. One has more than 800 entries in the vault. Another has almost 1,000. Others wrote 355, 400, more than 500, and some said they had trusted the app with their logins for about ten years. Each of them wanted to know the same thing, whether this meant all of them.

Reporters asked mSecure what had happened and got no answer. Today, four days after the email, the website and the blog still say nothing about it. In the forum threads full of worried customers, I could not find a single reply from the company.

The explanation came in a different way. Customers who opened a support ticket got an answer by email and pasted it into the forum. Several of them got exactly the same text.

In that reply, the company writes that an unauthorized party acquired an encrypted copy of a database containing information belonging to current and former users. The incident concerns customers who synced through mSecure Cloud, the company’s own sync service. They say they have no evidence that the confidential information inside was accessed, and no evidence that the app is unsafe to use today. item.title: Scamwich Fake Restaurant Ordering Sites
item.description:
820 fake ordering sites for 35 restaurant chains showed the restaurant’s own menu, then took the card and the bank’s text code. The customers did nothing wrong. Google ran the ads from July to October.

Someone wants lunch from Jimmy John’s. They type the name into Google instead of typing the web address, and at the top of the results sits a listing that looks like the restaurant’s own. The headline says something like Order Sandwiches for Pick Up, with a line about delivery, catering or a location near you. One click, and an ordering page opens with the sandwiches and the opening hours, and the prices match the restaurant’s.

They match because the fake site borrows them. Each time you click, it quietly asks the restaurant’s website for that same page, gets it back, puts its own web address where the restaurant’s was, and shows it to you. You are looking at the restaurant’s own page, passed through somebody else’s server. That setup is called a reverse proxy.

The scam runs on it.

So when the restaurant changes a price at noon, the fake site shows the new price at noon too. Even the restaurant’s own bot check keeps running on the page, because the fake site fixes its links so it still works. The researchers who found the network, at a company called InfoHawk, named it Scamwich and say the restaurant itself never had to be hacked.

Only one part of the page gets swapped. At checkout, the box where you type your card normally comes from the company that handles the restaurant’s payments. The fake site puts its own box there instead. A little script keeps an eye on the page, and if the original box comes back, it swaps that box out again.

A second script looks at the Place order button twice a second and copies the total. So the fake box shows the exact amount in your cart, down to the cent.

The address bar does not help you either. The sites sit behind Cloudflare, a service that hides where a website actually runs and gives it the file your browser checks before it calls a connection secure. That file is called a certificate, and these sites had valid ones. In the example the researchers show, the certificate came from Google Trust Services.

So the browser tells you the connection is secure. That only means outsiders cannot read what travels between you and the site. The site itself belonged to the scammers.

The fake box asks for the card number, the expiry date, the three digits on the back, your name and your phone number. The moment you press pay, those details go to the scammer, along with the name of the fake site.

The details arrive right away, over a connection between your browser and their server that stays open while you are on the page. The tool behind that is called socket.io. Someone on the other side can see your card as soon as you send it.

What happens next is what the researchers think this kit, the fake pages and scripts behind each site, was made for. A person sits behind a control panel and uses your card somewhere else.

Many banks ask for one more check when you pay online: a code by text message, or a tap to approve in your banking app. That way a card number alone is not enough. The check is called 3-D Secure. Here, it works against you.

Because when your bank sends that code, the scammer pushes a new page onto your screen. One page says the card was declined and asks for another. One asks for the code that came in on your phone. One asks you to approve the payment in your banking app. One says the code was wrong and asks you to type it again.

You type the code to pay for your lunch. According to the researchers, that code is what lets the scammer’s own purchase through the bank’s check. That is their reading of the kit; the report does not show a payment going through.

When the scammer is done, the page drops a small file in your browser, a cookie named valid with the value 77777, set to last until 2038. In the copy the researchers took apart, it then sends you on to the website of another chain, Jimmy John’s, through a link service called href.li that hides where you came from.

No order ever reaches the restaurant. You wait for food that is not coming, and according to the researchers your card has paid for whatever the scammer bought.

The researchers counted 820 of these fake web addresses across two rounds of searching, copies of 35 restaurant chains. 808 of them end in .delivery. That is the last part of a web address, like .com, and this one is official, added to the internet’s address system in 2014 and run by a company called Identity Digital. For a site where you order food, it sounds exactly right. The rest end in .com or .shop.

Jimmy John’s alone had 404 fake domains. Firehouse Subs had 121, with names like flrehousesubs.delivery, an l where the i should be. Jersey Mike’s had 80, among them mlckessejersstey.delivery and jerseymikes-delivery.com. Dave’s Hot Chicken had 67.

Waffle House got w0ffleh0use.delivery, with zeros for the a and the o. Chipotle, Popeyes, Panera Bread, Five Guys, Little Caesars, Tim Hortons and Wawa are on the list as well, some with a single copy, some with a handful. The earliest copy in the research turned up on March 3, 2026.

Almost all of them, 761 of the 820, sit behind that same service that hides their servers. Of the first 255 the researchers found, 251 were bought from the same shop for web addresses, Dynadot. A shop like that is called a registrar.

One server had a live card panel on it, the place where the card details arrive. A second group of 68 domains is tied to a server on Amazon’s cloud, and some of those sites run straight from it, in Frankfurt, with a slightly different script. The researchers found nothing that shows the same people run both.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. A kit can be shared or sold. A server address tells you where a machine is rented, not who rents it. What we know for sure is how these sites work.

On November 4, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site.

To bring people to them, the scammers bought Google search ads. The researchers found at least 47 of them between July 7 and October 20, 2026. And they only looked up ads for the sites from their first search, so there were probably more.

The ads ran under 46 separate advertiser accounts with 43 different business names, and those names look unrelated to the chains: construction firms, a watch company, a reptile rescue. How the scammers got hold of those accounts, the researchers do not say. Most ads ran for one to four days, usually starting a few days after the domain was registered. The longest ran for 56 days, the next for 39.

Google publishes a report each year about the bad ads it stops. The one for 2025 came out on April 16, 2026. The company says it blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion ads and shut down 24.9 million accounts. Its systems caught over 99 percent of the ads that broke its rules before they were ever shown, the report says, and 602 million ads had to do with scams. It also says it checks who its advertisers are.

These 47 got through. Some stayed up for weeks.

An advertiser can pay Google to show an ad when someone searches for another company’s name. That search word is called a keyword, and Google’s trademark policy does not restrict using someone else’s brand there. Many of the ads also put the brand name in the headline itself, followed by words like Menu Items or Catering Menu.

The 20 Jimmy John’s ads did not. Their headlines said Sandwich Shop or Order Sandwiches for Delivery, so a trademark complaint from the chain would have found no brand name in the ad to point at.

Google has a second rule that needs no complaint at all. Its policy against misleading ads bans pretending to be another brand or business, in the ad or on the website behind it. It treats that as one of its most serious violations and can suspend the account without warning. These ads sent people to sites that pretended to be the restaurant. They still ran, most of them for a few days only.

The man whose company found all of this knows the ad business from the inside. Rob Leathern, its CEO and co-founder, was VP of Privacy and Security Product at Google and led Business Integrity at Meta, according to its own team page. The company sells tools to detect exactly this kind of clone, and the report ends with an offer to check whether someone is copying your brand.

The trick itself is older than this campaign. On February 24, 2023, the writer Cory Doctorow described searching for a Thai restaurant he liked in Burbank, Kiin Thai. He clicked a sponsored result for a site called kiinthaila.com, built on Wix, while the restaurant’s own website was the third link down. The copy added 15 percent to the prices, passed the order on to the restaurant and billed him twice.

The restaurant called him to cancel and told him to contact his card company to get the charge reversed. That version still produced an order. The 2026 version produces none, shows the restaurant’s live menu instead of a copied one, and goes after your bank code too.

Two months before that post, on December 21, 2022, the FBI had already warned about this. It wrote that criminals were buying search ads with web addresses that look like a known business. Those ads showed up at the very top of the results and looked almost the same as the normal ones. Its advice back then: check the address before you click an ad, type the address of a business yourself instead of searching for it, and use an ad blocker.

The chains in this campaign are American. A fake site that pulls the pages from the original and only swaps the payment box would work the same way for a pizza place in Rotterdam or a delivery service in Berlin.

By November 3, none of the ads the researchers found were still running, and Google’s own page for looking up ads now shows Can’t find ad for them.

Restaurants have one way to spot this early. The fake site has to ask the restaurant’s own server for each page. So a chain that watches for its pages showing up under a strange web address, or for checkouts that never reach its payment company, can catch these sites fast.

What you can do before you pay for food online:

  • → Type the restaurant’s address yourself, use a bookmark, or order through its own app
  • → Look at the domain in the address bar. A secure connection only tells you it is encrypted
  • → A brand name followed by .delivery, -delivery.com or -us.com was the pattern in this campaign
  • → Read the full text from your bank before you type a code anywhere. If the shop or the amount does not match your order, stop
  • → Pay with a credit card where you can, so you can dispute the charge
  • → Use an ad blocker, one of the tips from that 2022 warning
  • → If you typed your card into a site like this, call your bank, block the card, and in the US report it at ic3.gov

Want to see what a server in the middle can read? Run Burp Suite in your own lab and watch your browser’s traffic pass through. A second script looks at the Place order button twice a second and copies the total. So the fake box shows the exact amount in your cart, down to the cent.

The address bar does not help you either. The sites sit behind Cloudflare, a service that hides where a website actually runs and gives it the file your browser checks before it calls a connection secure. That file is called a certificate, and these sites had valid ones. In the example the researchers show, the certificate came from Google Trust Services.

So the browser tells you the connection is secure. That only means outsiders cannot read what travels between you and the site. The site itself belonged to the scammers.

The fake box asks for the card number, the expiry date, the three digits on the back, your name and your phone number. The moment you press pay, those details go to the scammer, along with the name of the fake site.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. A kit can be shared or sold. A server address tells you where a machine is rented, not who rents it. What we know for sure is how these sites work.

On November 4, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site.

Google publishes a report each year about the bad ads it stops. The one for 2025 came out on April 16, 2026. It also says it checks who its advertisers are.

These 47 got through. Some stayed up for weeks.

An advertiser can pay Google to show an ad when someone searches for another company’s name. That search word is called a keyword, and Google’s trademark policy does not restrict using someone else’s brand there. Many of the ads also put the brand name in the headline itself, followed by words like Menu Items or Catering Menu.

He clicked a sponsored result for a site called kiinthaila.com, built on Wix, while the restaurant’s own website was the third link down.
