item.title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infected Over 2,000 Windows Machines
item.description:
More than 2,000 Windows machines have been taken over by the security tools their owners cloned from GitHub and built themselves. The people getting hit are cybersecurity professionals, paid to stop exactly this. The fake repositories have been going up for two years, and some are still online today.

The trap works the way these people already work. A researcher needs a scanner, a reverse proxy, a script to clean up the output of another tool. They search GitHub, they find a repository that looks right, they clone it, and they build it. That last step is the one that ends it. The moment they build it, or even only open it, the machine is no longer theirs.

Doctor Web pulled the malware apart on November 5, 2026, and named the loader that runs it all Trojan.Loader.3261. The researchers found the malicious code hidden inside three kinds of project files, and each one fires in a different way.

In a Visual Studio C# project, the trap sits in the .csproj file as a pre-build event. A pre-build event is a command the project runs before the compiler even starts, meant for ordinary things like copying a file or stamping a version number. Here it runs a PowerShell command instead, the second the developer hits build.

In the same project there is a second file, the .suo, that holds another PowerShell command. The .suo lives in a hidden .vs folder that a developer rarely opens and that a file manager hides by default. In October 2023, Zhiniang Peng of Sangfor showed that a crafted .suo file can run code when a Visual Studio solution is simply opened, before anything is compiled at all. Microsoft did not treat that as a vulnerability. It said opening a project from an untrusted source is an insecure operation, and that users should turn on the trust settings to protect themselves.

The third path is for the Python and Go versions of these fake tools. There the malicious code is pushed far off the right edge of the file, behind a long run of whitespace, so a developer scrolling through the source sees a blank line and reads straight past it.

Once any of those three fires, a PowerShell script lands on disk and reaches out. It pulls an encrypted link from the attackers’ own servers and, alongside them, from ordinary places: YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. Traffic to those everyday sites looks like nothing on a corporate network. The decrypted link downloads an archive called Quixo.7z, which unpacks into a folder dressed up to look like a Windows photo component.

Inside that archive sits Microsoft.exe, and this is the program that does the damage. Doctor Web found it at version 1.4.5. It is built with Electron, the same toolkit behind many everyday desktop apps, so on the machine it looks like one more normal program. Then it goes after the defenses, one by one. It turns off Windows Defender, User Account Control, the pop-up warnings, System Restore and the Volume Shadow Copy Service that backups lean on.

The loader goes further. It puts RegAsm.exe and dwm.exe on Defender’s exclusion list, so the code it later hides in them is never scanned. It tries to remove three security products, McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes. And it rewrites the Windows hosts file so the machine can no longer even reach the websites of antivirus makers. When it is done, the machine has no guard left and no way to call out for a new one.

Getting that code to run without setting off an alarm is a job on its own, and the loader has a trick for each guard. It makes its own process look like a child of explorer.exe, the program behind your desktop, so it passes for something Windows started itself. It flips a setting in the registry to slip past Smart App Control, the check that is meant to block untrusted apps.

Security tools work by hooking into Windows and watching what runs through. So the loader quietly pulls those hooks back out. It reads a clean copy of ntdll.dll, a core Windows file, straight from disk and uses it to undo them. It calls Windows directly, underneath the layer where the watching happens, a move known as Halo’s Gate. And it switches off two parts of Windows, called ETW and AMSI, that would otherwise let a scanner watch what is running. The payloads end up tucked inside trusted programs like RegAsm.exe and dwm.exe.

What it drops is built to pay off in more than one way. The loader installs two separate copies of the AsyncRAT backdoor. They are identical except for the network port each one uses, and the researchers say this could let two operators hold the same machine at once, each through its own port. One infected computer, two operators, neither of them the person who bought it.

Alongside the backdoors comes a clipboard stealer. It watches for a cryptocurrency wallet address being copied and swaps in the attackers’ address, so money meant for one wallet lands in another. On each swap it grabs a screenshot and sends it to a Telegram bot, together with the title of the active window, the username and the machine’s IP address.

The last piece is an information stealer, and what it goes after is exactly what sits on a security professional’s laptop. It checks first whether it is running in a sandbox or a virtual machine. If the coast is clear, it collects browser data, the saved sites and passwords in FileZilla, the MobaXterm.ini file full of saved SSH sessions, Total Commander’s FTP logins, VPN settings, messenger files, gaming accounts and Discord tokens. All of it gets packed up and sent out through the Telegram bot. These are the keys to other people’s networks, held by the people paid to defend them.

The campaign began somewhere else entirely. In the early days the fake repositories were bots and cheats for crypto games, including one built around the Telegram game Catizen, going after people chasing a quick token. For readers without the right setup, some of those repositories even walked them through installing Visual Studio and cloning the project, step by step.

At some point the operators turned toward a richer target and started dressing the same malware up as scanning tools, security testing tools and log analysis scripts. The researchers also found a component that is not finished yet, built to install the loader as a Windows service and re-download it if it is ever removed. Whoever runs this is still building.

These repositories are still out there. Checking the ones in Doctor Web’s published indicators this morning, two days after the report, several were still live. One is advertised as a lightweight script to parse and clean up the output of Fscan, a network scanner with nearly 15,000 stars that security testers rely on. Another lifts its description straight from a genuine open-source tool, so it reads as legitimate at a glance. Two of the nine example repositories now return a 404. The rest were still there.

Researchers have run into this same toolkit before. In June 2025, Trend Micro wrote about a campaign it called Water Curse, with at least 76 GitHub accounts pushing fake penetration-testing tools. It used the very same parts: a pre-build event in a .csproj, an Electron app, a scheduled task that relaunches a Microsoft.exe on a timer, code slipped into RegAsm.exe, and Telegram used the same way to carry the stolen data out.

The overlap runs down to the internal file names. Trend Micro found the same hidden modules in 2025, boot_f, kernel_f and thread_f, and could only guess what some of them did. Doctor Web has now taken the same pieces apart. The file names and the methods line up that closely, but that does not prove the same people are behind both.

In security, working out who did it is one of the hardest problems there is. Tools get shared, sold and copied, and the same tricks can belong to one group or to several using the same playbook. What we can be sure of is how the malware works, not whose hands are on the keyboard.

Hiding code behind a long stretch of whitespace is older still. In February 2025, Kaspersky wrote up GitVenom, hundreds of fake GitHub projects where the Python payload sat behind about 2,000 tab characters. One of the attackers’ wallets took in roughly 5 BTC, about 485,000 dollars at the time.

Handing a security researcher a Visual Studio project with a trap inside is an old idea. In January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group described a campaign it put down to a government-backed group in North Korea. The attackers made contact, offered to work together on research, and sent over a project with a malicious DLL wired to run through the build events. That is Google’s read on that 2021 case, and nothing here ties it to the GitHub campaign running now.

After that, Microsoft added a trust setting you can switch on, one that makes you approve a project from an untrusted source before it opens. It stays off unless you turn it on yourself. A warning that appears on its own came later, in Visual Studio 2022 version 17.12 from November 2024, and only when the file carries a Mark of the Web, the little tag Windows puts on anything you download. Code pulled straight down with git clone often has no such tag, so no warning shows up.

So the defense comes down to a habit. Before opening a cloned project, look inside the project file itself. In a Visual Studio project, open the .csproj in a plain text editor and check for a pre-build event you did not expect:

1
2
3

<Target Name="PreBuild" BeforeTargets="PreBuildEvent">
  <Exec Command="powershell -enc ..." />
</Target>

A line like that, calling PowerShell or a script before the code even compiles, has no legitimate reason to sit in a tool you cloned minutes ago. Older projects tuck the same command inside a plain <PreBuildEvent> tag, so look for either. Delete the hidden .vs folder before you open the solution, so a planted .suo cannot run. Scroll Python and Go files all the way to the right, past where the text seems to end. And do all of it on a throwaway virtual machine with a clean snapshot, never on the laptop that holds your working keys. Doctor Web published the full list of indicators, the four attacker domains, the IP addresses and the file hashes, in its malware-iocs repository, and its products detect and remove this family.

item.title: Windows Paint Had a Code Execution Hole and the Fix Microsoft Named Never Reached the Store
item.description:
One crafted file opened in Paint could run an attacker’s code. In all 6 countries checked, the Store had no safe Paint. Auto-updates did not help. The fix Microsoft named on October 13 never got there.

On November 5, a Windows 11 PC with automatic app updates switched on in the Microsoft Store showed no update for Paint. Its owner assumed Paint was fine, and then looked up the version in the app’s settings.

Paint was running version 11.2603.251.0. According to Microsoft’s own documentation, only 11.2609.401.0 or newer was safe. The PC belonged to the editor of a Windows news site.

Microsoft tracks the hole as CVE-2026-83844. A program keeps the data it works with in blocks of memory, and each block has a fixed size. When Paint opens a picture, it reads what is in the file into such a block and works from there. Reading past the end of that block, into memory that was never meant for it, is called an out-of-bounds read. A file made for exactly that makes Paint do it, and according to Microsoft that can end with an attacker’s code running on your PC.

Microsoft’s own example of an attack is ordinary. Someone talks you into downloading a specially crafted file from a website, and you open it. Microsoft does not say which file type does it. The person who found the hole reported it anonymously.

Microsoft published the hole on October 13, the second Tuesday of the month, the day it releases its monthly security updates. On the same page it named the Paint version that fixed it: 11.2605.91.0.

That version never showed up in the Store or anywhere else.

On October 30, someone asked on Microsoft’s own question and answer forum where 11.2605.91.0 could be downloaded. The newest Paint they could get was 11.2605.81.0. 40 people clicked that they had the same question. The only answer came from another user, who did not think the version existed and guessed it was a typo.

Somewhere before November 4, Microsoft changed the number. In the security data Microsoft publishes for scanners and IT tools, the fixed version was now 11.2609.401.0. Microsoft added no note about the change to the page. And that version was not in the Store either.

The Store’s own product catalog shows why the update did not come. On November 5 at 03:34 UTC, Brian Vitko, who builds device management software at the company RFF, asked that catalog which Paint packages it had. He asked for six countries: the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, India and Singapore. All six gave the same answer. The newest Paint was 11.2605.81.0. That is below the fix, so the Store had nothing better to install.

His two Windows 11 lab machines showed the same thing. Paint was on 11.2605.81.0 for each user, and as far as the Store was concerned, both machines were up to date. He then ran the update scan that company management tools use to push Store updates to their PCs, and watched Paint for four minutes. It stayed where it was.

item.title: Unlock Cars From a License Plate
item.description:
A photo of your license plate could open your car and start its engine from far away. The car’s locks had nothing to do with it. The way in was an admin password the carmaker had left in its own files.

Two security researchers, Shubham Shah and Sam Curry, spent time earlier this year on the connected-car systems behind two car brands, from two sides. Shah is a co-founder of the Australian security firm Assetnote, and he took the Australian side. Curry has been taking apart car systems for years, and he took the United States. The apps let an owner unlock the doors, start and stop the engine, sound the horn and find the car on a map. Both sign customers in through the same software. That software is where it all fell apart.

Start with what happens when you prove who you are to a car app. You open the app, type your email and password, maybe approve a second step on your phone, and the app gets a token. A token is a short code the server hands back that says this phone may send commands to this car. That sign-in work runs on a server the carmaker owns, built on a product called ForgeRock, now part of Ping Identity. It is an identity platform: one system that holds the customer accounts and decides who gets let in. Get into that one system as an administrator, and you stop being one customer. You become all of them at once.

On the Australian side, Shah started by mapping the carmaker’s web addresses. Big companies run far more than the one site customers see. They park internal tools and test systems on subdomains, the lesser-known addresses that hang off the main domain. While combing through the JavaScript files served from the carmaker’s own telematics domain, he found something that should never leave a developer’s laptop. One of those files, a bundle from an outside vendor, had a working administrator login for the identity server written straight into it. It was meant for a test setup. It worked on the live system too. The accounts of paying customers sat behind a password that was printed in a file the website served to the public.

This was not a sloppy company. Shah found the opposite: they had put a lot of work into firewall rules to block access to the sensitive parts. He respects the hardening, and suspects they knew how bad it was to leave this one system exposed, but that some business reason kept it there anyway. That is worse than a company that never noticed at all.

A web application firewall, or WAF, was supposed to sit in front of that identity server and block outside requests to the sensitive parts before they arrive. It did block the obvious paths. Shah and Curry sat stuck at it for days, until they let an AI model read the identity software’s source code for about six hours. The model found one path, /static, that slipped past the firewall where the others were blocked. The two of them had assumed, as people do, that one blocked path meant all of them were blocked. The server behind the firewall read that same address as a command, and from there the admin login did the rest.

On the United States side, the pair reached a hidden management console on the identity servers, a control panel meant only for the company’s own engineers. It still accepted the default username and password the software ships with. That default is public, and the maker’s own manual says to change it before the system goes live. It had not been changed. From that console Shah set up a scheduled task that ran his own code, which gave them command execution on the production server. Command execution means running programs on the company’s own machine, the one serving its customers, as if you worked there. An administrator on that identity server can read, change or delete a customer record and hand out a fresh session for it, and that is the level of access the two of them now had.

A single lookup, by email address or phone number, handed back the account’s password hash, its PIN hash, the push tokens tied to the owner’s phone, and the person’s full name and mobile number. Push tokens are the identifiers that let a service send notifications to a specific phone. A hash is a one-way scramble of the original value, so the password and the PIN did not come back as readable text. A weak PIN could still be guessed offline later. The push tokens, the number and the name needed no guessing: they sat there in plain form.

Taking over an account did not need the owner’s password at all. Through the admin controls, the researchers changed a chosen account’s email to one they held, then set a new password on it directly. When they signed in through the normal app, the system sent a six-digit verification code to the new email address, which they read. From there the app handed them the same token the owner’s own phone would get. On the owner’s side, nothing changed. Their existing app session stayed logged in while the researchers worked beside it, and once they had the tokens they set the original email back, so the account looked untouched. They could even register a push token of their own, so the alerts a car sends would reach them instead of the owner.

The second step that is meant to protect the account did not help either. In the Australian system, the code or the tap on your phone that normally stands between a stolen password and the account could be skipped through an old sign-in method that should have been retired years ago.

This is the part that reaches your own car in your own driveway. Your car carries a VIN, the vehicle identification number stamped on it at the factory and visible through the windshield. Someone walking past can read it off the glass. In Australia, a plate is enough on its own: it gives you the VIN through the state registration-lookup sites, and the admin tool turned a VIN into the exact account it belonged to. That lookup was a built-in part of the system meant for staff, which is why it answered without complaint. In the United States test, Shah checked a car with its owner standing beside it, then unlocked the doors, started the engine, shut it off and locked it again.

A few things keep this from being a nightmare. These were researchers working with permission. The owner in the test stood beside the car and chose a new password after it was done. The researchers did not name the carmaker in their writeups, because they were asked not to, and they held back the exact web addresses and credentials so others could not follow along. They give no number for how many cars or customers could have been reached, only that it would hit an owner who had the remote features switched on. The response was fast: once they reported it, the carmaker fixed it within about two hours, took down the test code, and changed the exposed passwords. The researchers were given no reward and no public credit for the work.

This is not the first time these two have walked into the car industry through the web instead of through the car. Over the past few years they found ways to reach vehicles from brands like Honda, Nissan, Hyundai and Ford, and later dug into Kia and Subaru. Four years ago, in that same stretch of work, they pulled a staging key out of the JavaScript on a Ferrari dealer web page and used it to reach Ferrari’s production systems. From there they could read, change or delete any customer’s account and change its role, and the dealer back office even handed back a set of live service credentials in plain text. Same mistake, a different brand: a test key left where the public could reach it.

Each time the way in was an account or dealer system, not anything mechanical on the vehicle. The finding keeps coming back the same way. The car itself is usually solid. The website and the app behind it are the way in, because they are built fast, wired to live customer data, and harder to lock down than the thing they control.

A few weeks ago I wrote here about how car apps quietly send your VIN off to advertising and tracking firms. It is the same number, pointed at a different danger. In that story it ties your car to your shopping and your movements. In this one it is the first link in a chain that ends with your doors open and your engine running. The number was never meant to be a secret. It is printed on the glass on purpose. That becomes the trouble when a login system treats something people can read off a parked car as something only the owner should know.

You cannot do much about a carmaker’s server, since that part is on them. What you can do is treat your VIN as more public than the apps pretend. Think twice before feeding it into lookup and valuation sites. And remember that the remote features in a car app are only as safe as the company’s weakest web address. This break-in did not need a cut wire or a scanner held near the door. It needed a laptop, a phone app read line by line, and a login the company forgot to lock. On a modern car, the account behind the app has become the way in, long before the lock on the door.

Want to see what your own car app sends the moment you press unlock? Route your phone’s traffic through a proxy you control and read it. item.title: Webloc Lets Police Track Phones Through the Ads in Weather Apps and Games
item.description:
Police bought a tool that shows where up to 500 million phones have been over 12 months, without a warrant. The location came out of the ads in weather apps, games and a prayer app. Up to 500 million phones sit in the tool they bought, on sale since 2020.

In 2025, a US firm prepared presentations for police forces in several countries to show what its tracking tool, Webloc, could do. On the screen, it followed people’s phones as they walked down Fifth Avenue in New York, visited the European Central Bank in Frankfurt and came close to the UK Parliament in London. Bloomberg News got hold of those presentations, along with training material and internal documents.

The seller is Penlink, which has made software for American police for decades, mostly to analyze tapped phone calls and internet data gathered during investigations. Webloc comes from Israel. It was built by Cobwebs Technologies, set up in 2015 by three veterans of Israeli special forces, who designed it for counterterrorism. In 2023 both ended up under the same US investment firm, and the sale of Webloc moved to the American side. A license starts at around 100,000 dollars a year.

In April, researchers at Citizen Lab, at the University of Toronto, mapped out what that money buys. They worked from contracts, procurement records and leaked documents, and describe access to records from up to 500 million mobile devices across the globe. In the documents the reporters saw, Webloc shows where a phone has been over the past 12 months, refreshed once an hour. One older US contract mentions three years.

An officer opens a map, draws a shape around a street or a building, and picks a time window. Webloc then lists the phones that were inside. It can show which phones turned up in two different places within the same window. It sends an alert when a phone shows up somewhere new, and it shows where a phone spends its nights and where it spends its days.

That last part is how police get from a phone to a name. A 2021 sales proposal for a police force in Central America puts it plainly: work out who is behind the device, find the home and the workplace, and send officers to the suspect.

To follow a phone, Webloc first has to recognize it, and for that it uses the advertising ID. Your phone has a number made for ads, on Android and on the iPhone. Apps read it so that advertisers can recognize the same phone across different apps and show it ads that fit. On an iPhone, an app has to ask your permission first.

The ad industry calls that number anonymous, because it carries no name and no phone number. A number that shows up at the same address night after night, and at the same office in the morning, still points to one person.

The researchers published what a single Webloc record could hold, as of 2021:

  • → the advertising ID and the IP address
  • → the time, plus GPS coordinates or a location worked out from nearby WiFi
  • → the name of the WiFi network the phone was connected to
  • → the brand, model and operating system of the phone
  • → an estimated home, workplace and most visited places
  • → age, gender, and labels such as parent, traveler or gamer
  • → the apps on the phone, with when each was first and last seen

Webloc’s makers say it now only holds locations tied to a device ID, with no age, gender or interests. The researchers had no way to check that.

A location can reach Webloc in two ways, and the researchers could not say for sure which one it uses today.

The first way runs through the app itself. A developer building a free app often adds ready-made code from an outside firm to show ads or to count users. That code is called an SDK, a software development kit, and it runs inside the app. Allow your weather app to see your location, and the code inside it can read that location too and pass it on to whoever wrote it.

One of those code makers is Start.io. According to the documents, its SDK sits in more than 500,000 apps with more than 25 billion downloads between them, and it claims to reach 2.4 billion devices, 300 million of them in the US. A platform that checks Android apps for trackers found one linked to it in more than 4,400 apps.

Some of the location data in Webloc came from there, according to the documents and former employees. Webloc’s makers deny buying it and say the Israeli developers only ran a trial with that data before the takeover. The SDK maker answers that its contracts limit the data to advertising, that most of it is not precise, and that the download figures are theoretical.

The second way needs no code inside the app at all. When an app has room for an ad, it sends out a request, and advertisers bid on it within a fraction of a second. That request can carry the advertising ID and the location of the phone, and those taking part in the auction get to see it. The stream of data from those auctions is called the bidstream. A data broker that joins in can collect locations from apps it never made a deal with.

That is why app makers often have no idea where their users’ locations end up. Webloc’s makers say their partners collect through their own SDK deals and get consent through the apps, but those partners do not hand over a full list of which apps. The seller itself is listed in California’s register of data brokers, and its own privacy policy says it may get a device’s past locations from other brokers.

One detail in the 2021 records points to the first way. They show the names of WiFi networks, and those names cannot travel through the ad auction, only through code inside an app. So back then, at least part of the data came out of the apps.

The documents do name apps: weather apps on Android and iOS such as AccuWeather, the prayer app Muslim Pro, downloaded more than 100 million times on Google Play, and the game Multi Maze 3D. All three deny any deal with the seller. The documents show where the data came from. They do not show who handed it over, and with a chain this hidden, the app makers may not know either.

The prayer app has been here before. In 2020, reporters found it was sending precise location data to a broker, and that broker confirmed to a US senator that it sold data from US phones to US military customers through defense contractors. The app called the report incorrect and cut its ties with its data partners. In January 2025, hackers stole files from another location broker, Gravy Analytics, including a list of thousands of apps its data came from. The prayer app was on that list too, and said it does not allow the ad networks it works with to collect location.

Police can buy this because of a gap in the law. In 2018, the US Supreme Court ruled that police need a warrant from a judge to get someone’s location history from a phone company. Since then, the Justice Department has argued that this rule does not cover location data that police buy on the open market. Asking a phone company needs a judge. Buying the same kind of data from a broker, in that reading, does not. So in most of the US, Webloc is used without a warrant.

In June 2026, the court went a step further. It ruled in a new case that getting someone’s location history from Google counts as a search, because people can reasonably expect the location of their phone to stay private. The ruling says nothing about buying data from brokers. Some privacy lawyers say those purchases now stand on weaker ground, while a former official of that same department writes that the ruling leaves them untouched.

Who uses it:

  • → US Immigration and Customs Enforcement spent around 9 million dollars on four contracts between 2022 and 2026, which included Webloc licenses, according to US procurement records
  • → at least two branches of the US military
  • → more than a dozen US police forces, including Dallas and Baltimore
  • → the Los Angeles police, who ran 136 searches in 2022 and 1,319 in 2023 in Webloc and its sister tool Tangles combined
  • → Hungary’s domestic intelligence, since at least 2022, which the researchers call the first confirmed use of this kind of ad-based tracking in Europe
  • → the national police of El Salvador, who bought it together with two other tools from the same maker through a Mexican reseller, and used it in 2021

Sales records and insiders show that Webloc has also gone to London’s Metropolitan Police and to authorities in Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Mexico, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, the Netherlands and Germany.

The police in Tucson signed a contract with Webloc’s makers, paid with border security money meant for sex trafficking investigations. In September 2023, an internal police report described how they used Webloc in a case of thefts and burglaries, and found the apartment of the suspect and his partner. The police say their license has since expired.

The ATF, the US agency for firearms and explosives, ran more than 340 searches in Webloc without a warrant, according to two members of the US Congress. More than 222 of them were tied to active cases. In a suspected arson at a defense contractor, a prosecutor and a judge were uneasy about using this kind of ad data, and the agency asked a court for phone tower records instead. After the two lawmakers started asking questions, the agency cancelled the contract in June and said the tool did not meet its needs.

In training sessions, the seller’s staff showed police how to follow people at pro-Palestinian demonstrations, suspected Iranian spies, Serbian militia groups and members of motorcycle gangs such as the Hells Angels, according to the documents. The seller’s answer is that the agencies ask for those examples themselves, and that using an example in a training is not the same as approving of it.

Webloc only goes to law enforcement and public safety agencies, and in rare cases to government contractors working for them, according to the seller and the investment firm behind it. The investors say it has helped find missing children, bank robbery suspects and trafficking networks. The seller says its data partners get consent and leave out hospitals, schools and places of worship.

That consent usually sits in the app’s terms. Those terms often say the developer may share location data with third parties. They do not say that a third party may sell it on to a police tool.

To the Toronto researchers, the seller replied that their findings rest on wrong information or a misunderstanding, and describe products that no longer exist. Which products, it did not say.

The documents also describe Safeloc, a version of Webloc meant for banks and retailers, for fraud checks and credit risk. The seller says no such product is on offer and that the material was probably made to test the idea. A security consultant working for the wine and spirits arm of LVMH showed how Webloc could help investigate thefts at a warehouse in western France, French reporters revealed this summer. The consultant says the luxury group chose not to use it, and the investors behind Webloc say they never sold it to the group.

In 2025, Montana became the first US state to ban its own police from buying location data on the open market without a warrant or a subpoena from a court.

In January 2025, the FTC, the US agency that protects consumers, banned the broker whose files had leaked that month, and its subsidiary, from selling sensitive location data. According to the agency, the two claimed to process more than 17 billion signals from around a billion mobile devices a day. The ban has an exception for national security and law enforcement.

A federal bill to close this gap passed the US House of Representatives in 2024, but never got a vote in the Senate. The same idea is now in a new surveillance reform bill, which has not come to a vote either.

What you can do on your own phone:

  • → On an iPhone, go to Settings, Privacy & Security, Tracking, and switch off Allow Apps to Request to Track
  • → On Android 12 or newer, go to Settings, Privacy, Ads, and tap Delete advertising ID
  • → Go through the location permission of each app, and give it only while using the app, or not at all
  • → Remove free apps you no longer use

These steps cut down the sharing, but they do not close it. Google’s own rules for app developers allow an app to fall back on its own identifier when the advertising ID is gone.

Want to see which servers a free app contacts? Run Android in VirtualBox, open the app, and watch its traffic in Wireshark.
